question_text: Why can't aromatic primary amines be prepared by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis?

mark_split.label: Why the C–X bond does not break

ORGANIC CHEMISTRY"); the book prints this question on book p.116 as VSAQ 9. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK CHECK: the printed reason — potassium phthalimide does not react with an aryl halide because the C–X bond in a halo arene has partial double bond character — is CORRECT and is kept. BOOK TYPOS on the same answer: "pthalimide" for phthalimide (used twice), "don't reacts", "Aramatic", and "can't prepared". BOOK GAP, filled here: the printed answer does not say that a BENZYLIC halide such as benzyl chloride DOES react, because there the halogen sits on an sp³ carbon outside the ring; benzylamine is therefore obtainable by this synthesis even though aniline is not.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The step that fails
lines: phthalimide to replace the halogen of an
An aryl halide does not undergo this
steps.why: Every Gabriel synthesis begins with the phthalimide anion replacing a halogen. If that one step does not take place, no N-aryl phthalimide is made, and there is nothing to hydrolyse in the last step. The synthesis stops at the very first arrow.
common_mistakes: Saying the hydrolysis step fails. The failure is at the substitution step, before any N-substituted phthalimide exists.
Writing that phthalimide is not nucleophilic enough. The phthalimide anion is a good nucleophile; the aryl halide is the part that will not react.
steps.memory_tip: The synthesis begins with a substitution on the halide, so a halide that will not substitute stops it at step one.
steps.margin_note: Write "no reaction" beside the equation. Naming which step fails is the first mark.

lines.text: C–X has partial double bond character

lines: So the C–X bond is shorter and stronger
than in an alkyl halide and is hard to break.
The ring carbon is also sp² and its π
So the halogen must be on an sp³ carbon.
Benzyl chloride works, because its halogen
is outside the ring on an sp³ CH₂ carbon.
Benzylamine can be made; aniline cannot.
steps.why: Delocalisation of the halogen lone pair into the ring gives the C–X bond some double bond character, which shortens and strengthens it. A stronger bond needs more energy to break, so the substitution that Gabriel synthesis depends on does not take place under these conditions.
common_mistakes: Saying the C–X bond in a halo arene is weaker. It is stronger and shorter than in an alkyl halide, which is why it does not break.
Claiming no benzene-containing amine can be made this way. Benzylamine can, because benzyl chloride carries its halogen on an sp³ carbon.
steps.memory_tip: The halogen lone pair goes into the ring, so the C–X bond gains double bond character and will not break.
steps.margin_note: The phrase partial double bond character is the marked phrase. Write it in those words.

insider_note: The examiner is looking for one phrase: the C–X bond in a halo arene has partial double bond character and does not undergo nucleophilic substitution. Adding that benzyl chloride does react shows the limit is about the sp² ring carbon, not about benzene rings in general.
